## Question 1 (Test Outcomes)

a) If my test has 70% power and an $\alpha$ of .01,{{< hp glyph="a" >}} what are my chances of making a Type I Error and a Type II Error?

b) If I wanted to reduce my chances of making each type of error,{{< hp glyph="a" >}} what could I change about my study/analysis?

## Question 2 (Single sample $t$-test)

a) My friend is arguing that professors (across all ranks and disciplines) make, on average, $100,000 per year. This doesn’t sound right to me, so I want to approach this statistically.{{< hp glyph="a" >}} What should I use as my null hypothesis and what should I use as my alternative hypothesis?

b) Conduct a one-sample $t$-test to test the null hypothesis from part (a). Download and use the `salaries` data file and provide both the $p$-value and your decision whether to retain or reject the null. (Note that the salaries are given in thousands of dollars per year such that 120 would actually mean $120,000 per year.)

## Question 3 (Interpretation)

a) What was the observed test statistic from Question 2b and what were its degrees of freedom? (*Optional Challenge:* What was the critical value for that test?)

b) What does the $p$-value in this test mean? How can we interpret it statistically? Your answer should go beyond merely stating whether it was significant.

## Question 4 (Correlation Theory)

a) What does it mean for two variables to be positively or negatively correlated with one another?{{< hp glyph="a" >}} What does it mean for two variables to have a correlation close to zero?

b) Look at the following scatterplots and indicate whether you think the Pearson correlation for each would be positive, negative, or close to zero. Also indicate whether you think each relationship depicted is linear, nonlinear, or none.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5

library(tidyverse)
library(faux)
library(patchwork)

rsim <- function(r) {
  rnorm_multi(n = 200, vars = 2, mu = 0, sd = 1, r = r) %>% 
    as_tibble() %>% 
    rename(x = X1, y = X2)
}

set.seed(2021)
d1 <- tibble(
  x = rgamma(300, 1, 1),
  y = rnorm(300, 0, 5)
)

d2 <- tibble(
  x = runif(300, -3, 3),
  y = 1 / (1 + exp(-x * 4)) + rnorm(300, 0, .03)
)

d3 <- tibble(
  x = runif(300, -pi, 2*pi),
  y = cos(x) + rnorm(300, 0, 0.3)
)

d4 <- rsim(-0.8)

p1 <- ggplot(d1, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point()
p2 <- ggplot(d2, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point()
p3 <- ggplot(d3, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point()
p4 <- ggplot(d4, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point()
(p1 + p2 + p3 + p4) + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "i")
```

## Question 5 (Applied Correlations)

Download and read in the `factbook1M` dataset that contains information from the CIA’s World Factbook about all countries with more than 1 million people.

a) Calculate the covariance and correlation between the life expectancy (`life_exp`) and birth rate (`birth_rate`) variables.

b) Test whether this correlation is significantly different from zero at $\alpha=.05$. Report your results (including the test statistic, $p$-value, and confidence interval) and give a verbal interpretation (i.e., explain what it says about the relationship).
